title: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Visual Perception” (from p. 577), p. 582. Scope: human visual recognition of repetitive and nested two-dimensional patterns

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is clear and can be tested on existing pattern resources, with some relevant behavioral data publicly available. Full scope likely requires a purpose-built matched experiment, while computational recognizability alone does not test human vision.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure accuracy and response time for matched repetitive and recursively nested patterns while controlling uniform-area size, then compare human performance with pointer-based compression scores. A large selective human deficit for nesting supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A directly matched public human dataset may need compilation.

Performance depends on exposure duration and training.

Pattern families can differ in low-level visual statistics.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.78
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data existence: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast is experimentally sharp: periodic patterns versus nested patterns, with a simple encoder as the existence proof that the nesting is objectively present. Published work on symmetry detection covers the easy half. Public datasets do not contain a systematic human test of nested cellular-automaton patterns, so that half of the claim is only sparsely constrained.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Show observers two-dimensional patterns that are purely periodic or nested, excluding cases dominated by large uniform regions, and compare detection accuracy with a pointer-based encoder that flags the nesting. High accuracy for repetition and chance accuracy for nesting would support the claim; reliable visual detection of nesting would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Symmetry and repetition detection are well studied; nesting as Wolfram defines it is not a standard stimulus class in public archives.

A new forced-choice experiment would be new data collection, which is outside existing resources.

operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.44
